samples.summary: Entry-parity guard is a source-text regex, so it can go green while the real Node-entry import still fails
samples.evidence: The test never imports either entry; it regex-scans the source for `export { ... } from './store/block-helpers.js'` with single quotes exactly (line 19-20). Any other export form — `export * from './store/block-helpers.js'`, double quotes, or a helper re-exported through an intermediate module — is invisible to the browser-side scan, so a helper missing from `src/node.ts` would produce an empty diff and a passing test while `YorkieDocStore`'s import under Node still fails. A runtime comparison (`import * as browser from '../../src/index.js'` vs `../../src/node.js'`, comparing `Object.keys`) would test the actual failure mode rather than a textual proxy. Note the test does fail before this change's node.ts addition, so it is not vacuous — only weaker than it claims.

samples.summary: Parity guard only covers block-helpers exports; the other `@wafflebase/docs` symbols the Node-run store imports are unguarded against the same failure class
samples.evidence: `yorkie-doc-store.ts:27-41` imports `resolvePageSetup`, `normalizeBlockStyle`, `DEFAULT_BLOCK_STYLE`, `blockStyleId`, `materializeBlockSpacing` alongside the block helpers. The new test hard-codes `SOURCE = './store/block-helpers.js'` (entry-parity.test.ts:13) and skips every other specifier, so an index-only export of any of those symbols reproduces the exact bug this test was written for without failing.
